query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature stability of near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles is governed by a balance between the high configurational entropy that thermodynamically favors a uniform phase and kinetic effects arising from differential elemental diffusion. Nanoparticles that are synthesized to have a reduced proportion of fast-diffusing elements form more effective diffusion barriers (especially at grain boundaries), thereby impeding phase segregation and degradation under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles produced via physical or chemical synthesis methods, featuring an equiatomic elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Systematically modulate the synthesis by reducing the concentration of identified fast-diffusing elements (while compensating with a relative increase in slow-diffusing species so that the overall composition remains near-equiatomic) compared to a strictly equiatomic baseline.
generation.conditions: Testing under catalytic conditions at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric conditions at 473–1923 K in controlled reactive or inert atmospheres where surface diffusion plays a significant role.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and integrity of diffusion barriers at grain boundaries and within the nanoparticle matrix dictated by the distribution of fast versus slow-diffusing elements.
generation.mechanism: A lower fraction of fast-diffusing elements mitigates localized atomic rearrangements and diffusion that can lead to phase segregation. In contrast, an excess of fast-diffusing elements promotes rapid elemental rearrangements that overcome the stabilizing effect of high configurational entropy, thereby triggering segregation of secondary phases and degradation of the uniform solid-solution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with intentionally reduced fast-diffusing element content should exhibit a more uniform microstructure, less phase segregation, and preserved chemical composition during high-temperature exposure relative to a strictly equiatomic (baseline) composition. Conversely, samples with increased fast-diffusing species should display accelerated degradation and the emergence of secondary phases.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized with a strictly equiatomic composition without modulation of fast-diffusing element concentrations.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under high-temperature environments typical of catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) applications. It may not hold at ambient temperatures or under conditions where diffusion kinetics are significantly altered by the environment (e.g., very high or very low pressures or unconventional reactive atmospheres).
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold in fast-diffusing element concentration that separates stable from unstable nanoparticle behavior remains uncertain, as does the magnitude of the improvement in stability. Moreover, the influence of the specific elemental identities and possible synergistic effects between them are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: (1) a baseline group with strictly equiatomic composition and (2) an experimental group with a reduced concentration (by a controlled percentage, e.g., 10–20% decrease) of identified fast-diffusing elements while maintaining overall near-equiatomic ratios through compensatory adjustments of slower-diffusing species. Subject both sets to high-temperature conditions representative of catalytic and thermoelectric applications. Monitor structural and chemical stability over time using in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy.
measurements: In-situ high-temperature XRD to track phase evolution and the appearance of secondary phases
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural analysis
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for elemental mapping and detecting segregation at grain boundaries
Time-resolved measurements of particle morphology and compositional uniformity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with reduced fast-diffusing element content do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in structural uniformity and chemical stability compared to the baseline, or if an increase in fast-diffusing elements does not lead to accelerated phase segregation and degradation, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

frame.system: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by various physical and chemical fabrication approaches.
frame.goal: To elucidate the synthesis–structure–property relationships governing the structural and chemical stability of these nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) service regimes, including conditions where low noble-metal content is desirable.
frame.limitation: Existing studies have poorly established how fabrication influences the preservation of the solid-solution state during catalytic and thermoelectric operation; this obscures evaluation of their suitability and the mechanisms leading to either stability or degradation.
root_cause_cues: preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes
what governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability
constraints: Testing must consider operating temperatures: catalytic settings at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K
Catalysts should ideally have low noble-metal content
Controlled fabrication conditions to maintain near-equiatomic composition
frame.regime: High-temperature environments typical of catalytic operations (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric applications (473–1923 K).
prior_attempts: Multiple physical and chemical synthesis methods have produced these nanoparticles, yet none have established definitive links between fabrication variables and stability under service conditions.
Prior evaluations mainly report compositional and microstructural outcomes without a clear mechanistic explanation for stability loss or preservation.
frame.understanding: Mechanistic Hypothesis: The stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature conditions is governed by the competitive interplay between thermodynamic stabilization (via high configurational entropy) and kinetic effects (such as diffusion rates and localized atomistic rearrangements at grain boundaries). Specifically, nanoparticles that maintain a balanced diffusion barrier due to a particular distribution of fast- versus slow-diffusing elements will preserve their structural and chemical stability, while an imbalance (e.g., an excess of fast-diffusing species) will lead to phase segregation and degradation.

testable_hypothesis.intervention: Systematically vary the concentration of the fast-diffusing element(s) (while maintaining near-equiatomic overall composition) during synthesis. Compare thermal stability under controlled catalytic and thermoelectric test conditions to samples with a 'baseline' equiatomic distribution.
testable_hypothesis.predicted_observations: Nanoparticles with a reduced fraction of fast-diffusing elements will exhibit higher stability (i.e., less phase segregation, maintained uniformity in microstructure and composition) relative to the baseline. Conversely, an increased fraction of fast-diffusing elements will accelerate phase separation and lead to observable degradation (e.g., emergence of secondary phases, loss of equiatomic order).
testable_hypothesis.boundary_conditions: The hypothesis is constrained to service regimes at temperatures of 773–1173 K for catalytic applications and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications, under atmospheric or controlled reactive environments where surface phenomena play a role.
testable_hypothesis.connection_to_prior_evidence: This hypothesis integrates observed tendencies for phase segregation in nanoparticles lacking optimized elemental distribution, as reported in prior studies, by linking the diffusion behavior of individual elements to the overall phase stability of the solid-solution.
testable_hypothesis.falsification_test: If nanoparticles with an intentionally increased content of fast-diffusing elements do not show accelerated phase segregation or if altering the concentration of these elements does not produce a statistically significant difference in structural and chemical stability (as measured by in-situ high-temperature XRD or electron microscopy), then the hypothesis would be falsified.
